AGENTS.md’s layer diagram and licensing-rule gap are corrected.

It cross-links the older deep-research memory rather than duplicating it.

Next session should: read that memory file first, then work directly from the 5 new spec criteria (CRIT-LUMEN-170 through 174) plus the two HIGH findings — everything needed to resume is now in the repo, not just this conversation.

11	## Read this first if resuming Lumen work
12	
13	This session (2026-08-21/22) did three things in sequence: (1) fixed a large batch of real bugs found via rigorous real-data verification, rebuilt `lumen-cli` around `lumen-store`, and caught/reverted its own premature-versioning mistake (see [[feedback-no-premature-versioning-pre-release]]); (2) ran a full multi-dimensional codebase audit (architecture/security/performance/DX/bugs) via a `Workflow` with adversarial verification -- 17 findings raised, 16 confirmed real; (3) ran 5 parallel research forks on external prior art/crates to leverage instead of hand-rolling. The concrete backlog from (2) and (3) has been written directly into the relevant specs as new/corrected acceptance criteria (see "Where the backlog lives" below) -- **specs are the source of truth for what to implement next, this memory is the map + rationale.**
14	
15	## What's actually built and verified as of session end
16	
17	Commits this session, in order (all on `main`, nothing pushed to `origin`):
18	1. `3dbc83d` fix(lumen-model): real current-model pricing seeded, honest `is_fully_priced` signal replacing silent Sonnet-fallback substitution
19	2. `ab57d02` fix(lumen-session): ClaudeCodeAdapter per-turn economics (was one pre-summed synthetic turn), reasoning tokens, 5m/1h cache split wired from real data
20	3. `2d9c2ef` fix(lumen-session): OpenCodeAdapter fully rewritten against the real SQLite schema (was 100% fictional JSONL format, silently producing zero sessions)
21	4. `94f051c` feat(lumen-cli): rebuilt around `lumen-store` -- `ingest`/`sessions`/`session` replacing `trace`/`audit`/`scan`, which never touched the store
22	5. `1554c23` fix(lumen-session): missed `codex.rs` field addition from commit 1 (mechanical follow-up)
23	6. `db0c4b1` fix(lumen-session): CodexAdapter's `model_family` default no longer collides with a real seeded pricing row
24	7. `ae75c3a` fix(lumen-store): real command-argument redaction implemented (was zero implementation despite the spec's claim) + 7 weak store tests strengthened
25	8. `0433201` / `b6a5f67` feat + revert: `ReadContractEnvelope`/JSON schema wire-versioning -- built then reverted same session, see the premature-versioning lesson
26	9. `4176a77` refactor(lumen-store): versioned migration chain (V1-V7 + tracking table) collapsed to one idempotent schema script -- same lesson
27	
28	All verified via `cargo test --workspace` (30/30 green), `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` (clean), `cargo fmt --all -- --check` (clean), and real local session data across all 4 providers (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, AGY -- confirmed via actually running `lumen ingest`/`sessions`/`session` against real files on this machine, not just synthetic fixtures).
29	
30	## Where the backlog lives (specs, edited 2026-08-22 to capture today's decisions)
31	
32	- **`specs/SPEC-LUMEN-001-MODEL.json`**: `CRIT-LUMEN-008` corrected (no longer mandates the Sonnet-fallback behavior that was actually removed as a real bug fix -- the spec was contradicting shipped code). New `CRIT-LUMEN-170` (pricing data should be vendored from LiteLLM's `model_prices_and_context_window.json`, not hand-typed Rust literals -- NOT YET IMPLEMENTED). New `CRIT-LUMEN-171` (cost representation needs a proper sum type instead of `(f64, is_fully_priced: bool)` -- NOT YET IMPLEMENTED, exact Rust shape deliberately left open).
33	- **`specs/SPEC-LUMEN-002-SESSION.json`**: New `CRIT-LUMEN-172` (formalize the "unknown-model placeholder" convention as a real `SessionAdapter` trait contract + a machine-checked golden test per adapter, not scattered comments -- this is what let the `claude.rs` HIGH bug below go unnoticed). New `CRIT-LUMEN-173` (shared JSONL line-reading helper to de-duplicate `claude.rs`/`codex.rs`/`agy.rs`'s copy-pasted boilerplate -- NOT YET IMPLEMENTED, low priority).
34	- **`specs/SPEC-LUMEN-003-STORE.json`**: `CRIT-LUMEN-037` corrected with the real redaction fix design (shlex/shell-words tokenization + entropy-based secret detection, not "starts with `-`"). New `CRIT-LUMEN-174` (decide: wire the 6 unused repositories into `lumen-cli`, or explicitly defer them like the daemon -- genuinely undecided, needs a call before it's "resolved").
35	- **`AGENTS.md`**: layer diagram now includes `lumen-store`/`lumen-fixtures` (Layer 2.5, was missing entirely). Layer-licensing rule now has an explicit **unresolved** dev-dependency gap noted (`lumen-session`'s dev-deps pull in FSL-licensed `lumen-fixtures`→`lumen-store`) -- pick one of two fixes next session (carve-out the rule, or split the test fixtures into their own crate).
36	
37	## The two HIGH-severity findings to fix FIRST, independent of everything else
38	
39	1. **Security, `crates/lumen-store/src/repositories/command_event.rs:33`**: `redact_args`'s "starts with a single `-`" heuristic lets real secrets through unredacted (`--api-key -sk-live-abc123SECRET` and `mysql -pMySecretPassword123` both reproduced verbatim). Not live in the shipped CLI yet (no `lumen-cli` caller for `CommandEventRepository`), but it's the tested security boundary and will leak the moment a caller is wired up. Fix design is now in `CRIT-LUMEN-037`.
40	2. **Bug, `crates/lumen-session/src/adapters/claude.rs:37`**: `ClaudeCodeAdapter` still defaults `model_family` to `"claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022"` -- a real seeded pricing row -- exactly the bug class fixed in `CodexAdapter` (commit `db0c4b1`) but left unfixed in its sibling. An assistant turn with real usage but no `model` key silently prices at real Sonnet rates with `is_fully_priced: true`. **This is live in the most-used adapter today.** One-line fix: change the default to an honest placeholder (`"claude-code-unknown-model"`), following the convention `CRIT-LUMEN-172` is meant to formalize.
41	
42	## Full audit findings (16 confirmed, adversarially verified against real code)
43	
44	MEDIUM: layer-licensing violation (dev-deps, noted in AGENTS.md above); 6-of-7 `lumen-store` repositories orphaned/unwired (`CRIT-LUMEN-174`); `pricing.rs`'s `^\d+[A-Za-z]$` normalization rule could silently misprice a real distinct SKU shaped like `gemini-3.7-flash-8b` (Gemini 1.5 Flash-8B precedent -- not currently live, no such row is seeded); 6 unused dependencies across 3 crates (`rayon`/`memmap2` in lumen-analysis, `smallvec`/`tracing` in lumen-store, `simd-json`/`memmap2` in lumen-session -- three of these contradict their crate's own stated design); undocumented adapter-placeholder convention (`CRIT-LUMEN-172`).
45	
46	LOW: 3 avoidable per-turn allocations (`circuit_breaker.rs:36`, `pr_link.rs:47`, `flow.rs:27`); `lumen-cli` opens each ingest file twice (`main.rs:108`); `cmd_ingest` processes files strictly sequentially despite an unused 16-connection pool (`main.rs:275`); JSONL line-reading boilerplate duplicated across 3 adapters (`CRIT-LUMEN-173`); `AGENTS.md`'s layer diagram gap (fixed this session).
47	
48	Full findings with file:line evidence and adversarial-verification reasoning are in the workflow's journal at `/Users/gabe/.claude/projects/-Users-gabe-Projects-lumen/838a26ab-646c-45ac-8200-638bc101304a/subagents/workflows/wf_c9ac1746-5b6/journal.jsonl` if the exact verifier reasoning is ever needed again -- but the spec edits above already carry forward everything actionable.
49	
50	## External research findings (2026-08-22, 5 parallel forks, crate/tool claims verified live not recalled)
51	
52	- **Pricing data**: no viable Rust crate exists (checked `llm-pricing`/`ccost`/`llm_usages` -- all tiny single-maintainer side projects). **LiteLLM's `model_prices_and_context_window.json`** (BerriAI/litellm on GitHub) is the real answer -- actively maintained, 300+ models, and its `cache_creation_input_token_cost_above_1hr` field already matches our exact 1h-cache-tier need (cross-checked against real Opus 5 rates, matched exactly). → `CRIT-LUMEN-170`.
53	- **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions**: token-usage attribute naming aligns well with our `TurnTokenUsage` shape (real, maintained Rust crate `opentelemetry-semantic-conventions` v0.32.1 exists for attribute constants). But **cost/pricing is explicitly NOT covered** by the standard (left to the consumer entirely), and **model-name normalization is explicitly NOT covered either** (the standard's guidance is the opposite of ours: preserve the vendor string verbatim, never normalize). Both of Lumen's hardest, most bug-prone subsystems have zero prior art to lean on -- confirmed genuinely ours to design well, not something we're failing to find.
54	- **Redaction**: `shlex`/`shell-words` (real, maintained) fix the tokenization bug (naive `split_whitespace()` mis-splits quoted arguments). The actual redaction *signal* should be entropy-based secret detection (how gitleaks/`ripsecrets`/trufflehog work -- flag by character-shape, not token position), not "starts with a dash." Langfuse's documented masking approach validates keeping flag names visible and redacting only values (our existing instinct was right; only the signal was wrong). → `CRIT-LUMEN-037`.
55	- **SQLite migrations**: `rusqlite_migration` (3.86M downloads, actively maintained, `PRAGMA user_version`-based) and `refinery` (9.5M downloads, multi-backend) are both real and well-maintained, but both solve the *versioned migration with data preservation* problem -- exactly what we correctly decided we don't have yet. **Confirmed: keep the current one-idempotent-script approach.** Plan around `rusqlite_migration` specifically (not `refinery`) once there's a real installed base to protect.
56	- **Session/trace schema prior art**: Langfuse/LangSmith/OTel GenAI all model this as **nested spans** (tool calls as children of a turn/generation span with their own timing), not a flat list. Our `CanonicalTurn.tool_calls: Vec<...>` is flatter than all three references -- a real structural gap if per-tool-call latency/error ever matters, not urgent to fix now. For the adapter-consistency problem specifically: OTel's actual mechanism isn't a trait/doc-comment, it's **Weaver** -- a schema registry validated against real emitted output in CI. `CRIT-LUMEN-172` should be implemented Weaver-style (a golden/contract test per adapter), not just a doc comment.
57	
58	## Recommended next-session order
59	
60	1. Fix the two HIGH findings (`claude.rs:37` default, `redact_args` entropy-based rewrite) -- both are small, independent, and one is live in production data paths today.
61	2. Implement `CRIT-LUMEN-170` (vendor LiteLLM pricing data) -- directly prevents this session's core failure class (stale hand-typed rates) from recurring.
62	3. Implement `CRIT-LUMEN-172` as a real golden-test-per-adapter contract, not just a doc comment.
63	4. Design and implement `CRIT-LUMEN-171` (the `Pricing` sum type) -- bigger, touches the public API surface of `lumen-model`, do this after the above land and are stable.
64	5. Resolve `CRIT-LUMEN-174` (wire the 6 orphaned repositories into `lumen-cli`, or explicitly defer -- genuinely undecided, ask the user or make the call and document it either way).
65	6. Lower priority, whenever convenient: the 3 per-turn allocation fixes, the double-file-open in `main.rs:108`, `CRIT-LUMEN-173`'s shared JSONL helper, the 6 unused dependencies, the layer-licensing dev-dependency decision.
66	
67	See also [[project_lumen_adapter_accumulator_real_data_gaps]] (deep historical research context this session built on) and [[feedback_no_premature_versioning_pre_release]] (the standing rule that killed the migration-chain/ReadContractEnvelope over-build this session).

schema_migrations tracking table, and per-version apply/skip logic) into
MigrationManager::SCHEMA: one script, applied idempotently on every

all. Changing a column or table now means editing the relevant CREATE
statement directly; a local dev database that predates a schema change is
safe to delete and let this recreate, since nothing here needs to preserve
real user data yet. StoreError::MigrationFailed drops its now-meaningless
version field. SqliteStore::run_migrations returns () instead of an applied
count that no longer has meaning for a single-script model.

fix(lumen-store): implement the entropy-based redact_args fix design (CRIT-LUMEN-037)

redact_args tokenized on plain whitespace and treated any token starting
with a single '-' as an opaque, always-preserved flag -- "starts with -" is
a CLI-parsing convention, not a security boundary. Reproduced with real
inputs: "--api-key -sk-live-abc123SECRET" and "mysql -pMySecretPassword123"
both passed through with the secret-bearing token completely unredacted
(HIGH, audit 2026-08-22). Not live in the shipped CLI yet (no lumen-cli
caller wires CommandEventRepository), but it's the tested security boundary
and would leak the moment a caller is wired up (see CRIT-LUMEN-174).

Replaces it with the fix design already recorded in the spec: shlex-based
real shell-word tokenization (falls back to a whitespace split only if the
input isn't valid shell syntax, so a malformed string still gets fully
redacted rather than erroring out unsanitized), and shape-based secret
detection -- Shannon entropy plus a known secret-prefix allowlist (sk-,
ghp_, AKIA, xox, etc., the gitleaks/ripsecrets/trufflehog model) -- instead
of dash-position. Flag names still round-trip verbatim; only the signal for
"is this a value" changed.

Adds three tests: the two real-input scenarios from the audit finding, and
a quoted-multiword-argument case proving the shlex tokenization half of the
fix (a naive whitespace split would mis-split it and leave literal quote
characters in the persisted output).

feat(lumen-model): vendor LiteLLM pricing data instead of hand-typed literals (CRIT-LUMEN-170)

PricingTable::seed()'s per-model dollar rates were hand-typed Rust
literals -- the staleness of hand-typed literals was the direct cause of
CRIT-LUMEN-008's real overcharge/undercharge bug (every current real model
mispriced against Sonnet's fallback rate). Research confirmed no viable
Rust crate exists for multi-provider LLM pricing, but LiteLLM's
community-maintained model_prices_and_context_window.json does, and cross-
validated exactly against Lumen's hand-typed rates for every field it
publishes.

Adds crates/lumen-model/data/litellm_model_prices.json (vendored via
`just update-pricing`, never fetched live -- Lumen prices historical
sessions and needs point-in-time-stable rates) and
pricing_source::load_vendored_rates, which loads it into PricingRate rows:
only "mode": "chat" entries under a direct first-party litellm_provider
(anthropic/openai/gemini/vertex_ai-language-models -- the providers
Lumen's four known adapters actually draw from; gateway/regional resale
listings like bedrock_converse/azure_ai are excluded) are loaded, and a
pricing field LiteLLM omits produces no row rather than an invented one.

That last rule surfaced two real corrections vendoring makes vs. the prior
hand-typed approximations: gpt-4o and gemini-2.0-flash publish no
cache-write rate at all (previously assumed same-as-input; now correctly
0.0 per CRIT-LUMEN-161), and gpt-5.6-terra's cache-write rate is real and
distinct ($2.50/M, not $2.00/M as previously assumed). A small hand-typed
layer remains in seed() for models that were real and verified at some
point but have since rolled off LiteLLM's current snapshot entirely
(claude-3-5-sonnet, claude-3-5-haiku, qwen-2.5-coder, claude-opus v3,
deepseek-r1, kimi-k1.5, glm-4-plus, gemini-2.0-pro) -- a disappearance
from LiteLLM's *current* file must not make real historical sessions using
those models go unpriced.

Vendoring also gives previously-unrecognized real models (gpt-4o-mini,
gemini-2.0-flash-lite) their own real prices instead of the unrecognized-
model 0.0 fallback, and a real dated snapshot (gemini-2.0-flash-001) its
own point-in-time rate instead of collapsing onto the current family rate
-- both are correctness improvements, and the affected tests are updated
to assert the new (better) outcome rather than the old one.

rate_for/normalize_model_key/is_recognized's lookup logic is unchanged --
only seed()'s data source changed.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BJf5Gw6NFsgLYb3mSnnfbe
EOF
)"

feat(lumen-session): formalize the unknown-model placeholder as a trait contract (CRIT-LUMEN-172)

The "<provider>-unknown-model" convention (fixing a model_family default
that collides with a real seeded PricingTable row, so an unpriced session
doesn't silently price at a real model's rate) was never a formal
contract -- only inconsistently-restated comments in individual adapter
files, with zero mention in SessionAdapter's own trait definition. That's
exactly why ClaudeCodeAdapter's instance of this bug (fixed yesterday,
commit d337b90) went unnoticed: there was no shared, discoverable, or
machine-checked source of truth a new adapter author -- or a regression in
an existing one -- could be checked against.

Adds a doc comment to SessionAdapter (adapter.rs) stating the contract
explicitly as required behavior for every implementation, and a shared
golden test (test_adapter_unknown_model_contract.rs, Weaver-style per
CRIT-LUMEN-172's research) that exercises all 4 known adapters --
ClaudeCode, Codex, AGY via the shared SessionAdapter::parse_stream path,
and OpenCode via its own parse_database entry point (it implements that
instead of SessionAdapter, being SQLite- rather than JSONL-backed) -- with
a minimal input carrying no model field, asserting uniformly: model_family
follows the naming convention, PricingTable::is_recognized() is false, and
TokenEconomics.is_fully_priced is false. A 5th adapter added later without
a case in this test is missing required coverage, not silently compliant.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BJf5Gw6NFsgLYb3mSnnfbe
EOF

total_cost_usd while ignoring is_fully_priced -- exactly what let
ClaudeCodeAdapter's stale model_family default (a separate confirmed HIGH
bug) produce a real, silently-wrong cost with nothing catching it at the
type level.

SessionSummaryReadModel::cost(), whose Unpriced case must be matched to

computation/storage representation (turn summation and SQL persistence
both need the raw value regardless of pricing status) -- Cost specifically
targets the point a cost is surfaced to a human, per the criterion's own
scoping. Applied at lumen-cli's three display call sites.

One of those three (cmd_sessions, the `lumen sessions` table) turned out to
read total_cost_usd with NO is_fully_priced check at all -- a live bug,
not hypothetical. Tracing why led to a second, more severe bug in
lumen-store: is_fully_priced had no backing column in either the sessions
or token_usage table, so upsert_session/insert_token_usage never persisted
it and get_session/per_model_by_session hardcoded it back as `true`
regardless of the real value on every read. A genuinely unpriced session
round-tripped through the store and came back indistinguishable from a
verified $0.00 everywhere the store's read models were used -- the exact
CRIT-LUMEN-008 bug class this project has repeatedly fixed at the adapter
layer, alive instead at the persistence layer. Fixed in the same pass and
tracked as its own criterion, SPEC-LUMEN-003-STORE.json's CRIT-LUMEN-175:
adds is_fully_priced INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 to both tables, persists
and reads it correctly in both repositories, and adds the field to
SessionSummaryReadModel. Regression test:
test_session_repository_is_fully_priced_round_trips_through_store.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BJf5Gw6NFsgLYb3mSnnfbe
EOF
)"

## Summary

Landed 5 commits this session (all local, nothing pushed to `origin`):

1. `d337b90` — ClaudeCodeAdapter's dangerous model_family default (HIGH bug)
2. `754f487` — `redact_args` entropy-based rewrite (HIGH bug, CRIT-LUMEN-037)

4. `4627958` — Golden-test-per-adapter contract for the unknown-model convention (CRIT-LUMEN-172)
5. `f0bd454` — `Cost` sum type at the pricing display boundary (CRIT-LUMEN-171)

The last one turned up something worth flagging: while applying the `Cost` type to lumen-cli's display code, I found `lumen sessions` was reading `total_cost_usd` with **no `is_fully_priced` check at all** — and tracing that back, `is_fully_priced` had no backing column in lumen-store's database at all. It was never persisted on write and hardcoded back to `true` on every read, so any session with an unrecognized model would silently show `$0.0000` instead of "unknown" the moment it round-tripped through the store. Fixed both tables' schema, both repositories, and added a regression test — tracked as new criterion CRIT-LUMEN-175.

Verified throughout: 189/189 tests, clippy clean, fmt clean, `cargo deny` clean.

content.text:
## Summary

Every item from the 2026-08-22 audit backlog is now done or explicitly deferred with a documented reason. 6 commits landed this session, all local (nothing pushed to `origin`):

1. `d337b90` — ClaudeCodeAdapter's dangerous model_family default (HIGH bug)
2. `754f487` — `redact_args` entropy-based rewrite (HIGH bug, CRIT-LUMEN-037)
3. `859f421` — Vendored LiteLLM pricing data (CRIT-LUMEN-170)
4. `4627958` — Golden-test-per-adapter contract for unknown-model handling (CRIT-LUMEN-172)
5. `f0bd454` — `Cost` sum type at the pricing display boundary (CRIT-LUMEN-171)
6. `3419587` — Wired `ToolCallRepository` into ingest; explicitly deferred the other 5 unused repositories (CRIT-LUMEN-174)

On CRIT-LUMEN-174 specifically: I looked at all 6 unused repositories concretely rather than guessing. Five genuinely need new feature work with no existing caller (a findings/rule engine, a daemon, a rollup job, command-event extraction ToolIntent doesn't cleanly support) — deferring those is consistent with this project's own standing lesson against building speculative features. `ToolCallRepository` was different: its *read* side was already wired into `get_session` and already shipped in the CLI's output, so `tool_counts`/`error_counts` were an already-advertised feature that silently always returned empty. That's a real bug in shipped functionality, not unbuilt work, so I wired it — closing it with a real end-to-end test against a real fixture.

Two more real bugs turned up along the way (not from the original audit, found while implementing the planned criteria): CRIT-LUMEN-175 (`is_fully_priced` silently lost on every store round-trip) and this tool_counts gap. Both are fixed.

Verified throughout: 190/190 tests, clippy clean, fmt clean, `cargo deny` clean. Memory updated. Only the low-priority cleanup bucket remains (minor allocations, a shared JSONL helper, unused deps) — nothing urgent, no known live bugs.

Any outstanding bugs we've identified? Do we do another round of adversarial analysis looking for bugs? We're finding a lot which is weird given our plugins and our SDD workflow. That shouldnt' be happeneing. Did we not research appropriately? Are our specs not good enough? What's going on?

Short answer: no known live HIGH bugs remain — everything from the 2026-08-22 audit is done or explicitly deferred (see the memory file). What's left is a small low-priority cleanup list (3 minor allocation fixes, a shared JSONL helper, 6 unused deps, one dev-dependency licensing decision). But your instinct that this is worth interrogating is right, and I have real evidence from this session about why bugs kept surfacing.

**What was actually happening, by category — not vague hand-waving:**

1. **Unverified-against-reality spec claims (the historically biggest source).** Earlier sessions found OpenCodeAdapter's entire wire format was fictional — invented from general LLM-agent knowledge, never checked against a real `opencode.db`. A spec criterion can be perfectly testable and pass its own test while describing a world that doesn't exist, because the test's fixture was invented alongside the spec, not sourced from reality. `trace` is supposed to prevent this, but only if it's actually pointed at real data — and it wasn't, for that criterion. This is largely fixed now (there's a standing memory rule about it), but it's the root cause of the largest bug class historically.

2. **Sibling drift — a fix applied once, not everywhere.** `claude.rs` had the exact same dangerous-default bug that `codex.rs` had already been fixed for. Nothing forced the fix to propagate to its three siblings. This isn't a research gap — it's a missing *consistency* mechanism. That's specifically why I built CRIT-LUMEN-172 this session (a golden test asserting all 4 adapters simultaneously): before that, nothing checked "does this same pattern exist elsewhere."

3. **Cross-layer round-trip gaps.** `is_fully_priced` and `tool_counts` are the clean example: the *read* side was built and shipped, the *write* side was never wired, and nothing broke because each layer's own tests only checked that layer in isolation. Specs here are organized per-crate (model/session/store) — nothing forces an explicit "does data survive the full write→persist→read path" test unless someone adds one. I found both by actually tracing real call sites while implementing something else, not via a dedicated bug hunt.

4. **"Marked done" without verification.** The redaction criterion was previously marked complete in the spec while having zero real implementation. That's axiom's job to catch — if the exit-gate isn't run rigorously per criterion, "spec says done" and "code actually does it" can diverge silently.

**Diagnosis:** graph→canon→vector→lambda→axiom is a "did we build what we said, correctly" pipeline — it verifies internal consistency against the spec, not external truth or cross-file consistency. `proof` is the actual adversarial bug-hunter, and it's a separate, opt-in tool, not something the SDD chain runs automatically. So finding bugs isn't evidence the workflow is broken — it's evidence `proof` hasn't been run against the code that's landed since the last pass, including everything from today (the Cost type, the pricing loader, the store schema changes, the tool_call wiring).

**Recommendation:** yes, run `/proof` now. A meaningful amount of new code landed today that's had TDD coverage but no adversarial pass, and proof specifically checks for sibling gaps — the exact category #2 above. Want me to kick that off?
How do we make sure our plugin pipeline is also considering architectural an semantic model issues? sibbling and cross-lay issues and gaps are flowing in

The core issue: `proof` (the adversarial/sibling-gap checker) is architecturally decoupled from the graph→canon→vector→lambda→axiom chain. Nothing in that chain runs it — it only fires when a human remembers to invoke it. And even within the chain, sibling-gap checking exists (`lambda:reviewer`, `lambda:exit-gate` both check for it) but is scoped to *one task's diff*, not "does this defect class recur across every implementer of this trait." Cross-layer round-trip properties fare worse — this project's specs are organized per-crate (model/session/store), so nothing ever asks "does this field survive write→persist→read across a crate boundary" unless a human thinks to write that criterion.

Three concrete ways to close this, in order of how structural a fix they are:

1. **Cheapest**: make `proof` a required checkpoint, not an optional afterthought — run it at the end of every implementation session (or every N commits), not only when something feels off. This alone would have caught today's sibling drift and the round-trip gaps sooner.
2. **Medium**: broaden what "sibling" means in the existing checks. `lambda:reviewer`/`lambda:exit-gate`'s sibling-gap check should explicitly ask "does this trait/interface have other implementers, and does this same fix apply to them" — not just scan the touched file's neighbors. Same idea for round-trips: `canon:audit-spec` could gain a 6th dimension — "does this criterion's data cross a crate boundary, and if so, is there a round-trip criterion covering the far side" — alongside its current five.
3. **Most structural**: whenever the *same* defect class gets fixed more than once across siblings (exactly what happened with the adapter default bug), that should automatically route to `canon:architect` to make the class impossible — a golden-test-per-implementer contract, a shared trait default, a sum type — rather than staying an ad hoc pattern I only reached for because I happened to notice it three fixes in.

Given ultracode isn't on for this session, I'd want your explicit go-ahead before building anything here — either (a) I write this up as a standing convention you apply manually, or (b) I build a `Workflow` script that composes `lambda`'s per-task output with a mandatory cross-implementer/round-trip sweep as a final phase, so it can't be skipped. Which direction, or something else?
We don't just want to catch it later in a proof run. The earlier we fix the issue the cheaper it is right?

Yes — and the useful move isn't "run proof earlier," it's asking *where each defect class actually gets introduced* and putting the check there instead.

**Sibling drift gets introduced at plan time, not code time.** The bug isn't "nobody caught it later" — it's that `vector:planner` decomposed "fix the model_family default" into one task, for one adapter, when the spec criterion was actually about a trait contract with 4 implementers. `vector:challenger` already has 7 review dimensions; it's missing an 8th: *when a task touches one implementer of a shared trait/interface, does the plan cover the others, or explicitly scope out why not*. That's checkable mechanically — grep the workspace for `impl SessionAdapter for`, diff against the plan's task list. Doesn't need proof at all; it's a plan-quality check, cheaper than a code-quality check.

**Cross-layer round-trip gaps get introduced at spec-decomposition time.** `is_fully_priced` broke because SPEC-LUMEN-001 (model), 002 (session), 003 (store) are crate-scoped, and nobody wrote a criterion saying "this field must survive store round-trip." That's a `canon:draft-spec`/`canon:audit-spec` gap: whenever a criterion introduces a field on a type that another spec persists or reads, the drafting/audit step should check the far-side spec for a matching round-trip criterion and flag it if missing — a 6th audit dimension alongside the existing five.

**But the actually cheapest fix, cheaper than any agent step, is type-level.** Notice what just happened in practice: the moment I added `is_fully_priced` as a real field on `SessionSummaryReadModel`, the Rust compiler refused to build until every construction site handled it — that's what caught all 7 sites instantly, for free, before any test ran. The *original* bug survived precisely because nothing forced that exhaustiveness — a hand-typed `is_fully_priced: true` compiled fine with no link back to "this column exists in the schema." So the real shift-left move for this category isn't a smarter agent, it's: whenever a domain field crosses a persistence boundary, make its absence a compile error, not a runtime maybe. That's `canon:architect`'s job today, but only reactively, after a pattern repeats. It should be the default posture whenever a spec criterion introduces a boundary-crossing field, not something we reach for after finding it twice.

Concrete proposal, cheapest-to-most-structural:
1. Add the "single-implementer fix for a multi-implementer defect" dimension to `vector:challenger`.
2. Add the "boundary-crossing field needs a round-trip criterion" dimension to `canon:audit-spec`.
3. Make "prefer a compile-time-enforced representation over a runtime check" the default instruction to `lambda:implementer` whenever a task's criterion is about data crossing a layer boundary, not just a `canon:architect` escalation path.

Want me to draft the actual instruction/prompt changes for these three, or is there a different point in the chain you'd target first?

Think broadly about TDD and SDD, agnostic of language too because we do code in TS and RS a lot but might need to dip into other languanges. We want to make sure we consider and present architectural issues, model issues, etc.

We should also consider that at the earlier spec and planning phase we need to collaborate a lot more with our human. Present proposals, explain research, tradeoffs, etc. Probably create artifacts for review to increase understanding. We want to improve the overall workflow but make sure we're not wasting output tokens. We want everything to be succinct, to the point and not waste words or create walls of text.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Workflow design note

Shift-left gates for the SDD pipeline

Architectural and semantic-model defects — sibling drift, cross-layer round-trip gaps — are cheaper to stop at spec and plan time than to catch in a later proof pass. Three insertions, language-agnostic, none of them new agents.

Where the pipeline stands today

proof stays — it's the backstop, not the plan

Where three real defects actually got introduced

From this session, not hypotheticals.

Lumen — traced back to origin
DefectIntroduced atWould've been caught by
ClaudeCodeAdapter defaulted to a real, priced model codex.rs already had this exact fix — it never propagated vector — plan Plan task for one SessionAdapter impl, not all four
is_fully_priced hardcoded true on store read-back no column existed; field silently defaulted every round-trip canon — spec Spec never asked "does this field survive the store crate boundary"
tool_counts always empty in shipped output read path shipped; write path never wired canon — spec Same boundary gap — the record type never carried what the read side needed

Three insertions

Language-agnostic — the mechanism differs per stack, the question doesn't.

01

Interface-completeness check

When a task touches one implementer of a shared trait / interface / protocol, the plan must cover every other implementer, or state explicitly why not.

Lives in: vector:challenger, as an eighth review dimension. Mechanical, not judgment — enumerate implementers, diff against planned tasks.
02

Boundary round-trip check

When a criterion introduces a field on a type another spec persists, serializes, or transmits, that far-side spec needs a matching round-trip criterion — or the gap is named on purpose.

Lives in: canon:audit-spec, as a sixth audit dimension alongside its current five.
03

Default to unrepresentable-by-construction

A value that's sometimes absent, sometimes wrong, or sometimes stale should be a sum type / discriminated union / Result by default — not a bool sitting next to a number, checked by convention. Applies equally to a Rust enum, a TS discriminated union, or a sealed class elsewhere.

Lives in: lambda:implementer's default posture for boundary-crossing fields — reach for this before canon:architect is escalated to, not after.

Where the human sits

Two required pauses — both before a line of implementation code exists.

01
canon drafts + gates a spec
research-report and tradeoffs attached, not just the passing criteria
GATE
Publish spec + tradeoffs as an artifact
short comparison table, not prose — sign-off before vector plans anything
02
vector plans + challenges
interface-completeness check runs here
GATE
Publish plan + task table as an artifact
sign-off before lambda writes anything
03
lambda → axiom → proof run to completion
no further pause — this part was already trustworthy

Token discipline

Tables, not paragraphs

Tradeoffs as a comparison grid. Findings as criterion_id / type / fix rows, matching canon's existing issue format.

One diagram, not a narrative

A plan is a task list a human can scan in ten seconds — not a chat transcript reconstructed as prose.

Flag, don't restate

Checkpoint artifacts show deltas and open questions — never the full spec text the human already saw.

Pick a starting point: draft the vector:challenger dimension, the canon:audit-spec dimension, or the lambda default-posture instruction — or pilot the two-gate checkpoint manually on the next spec before wiring any of it in.

I found comprehensive information about spec drift, living specifications, and agentic development. Here's what the search results reveal:

## Spec Drift in Agentic Development

Static specs drift as code and dependencies change, which is a core problem in AI-assisted development. The issue manifests when the markdown says one thing, the repository says another, and the next regeneration cycle amplifies the mismatch.

A study of failed AI-generated PRs found that alignment loss during execution caused more failures than incorrect task descriptions, highlighting that the root cause isn't just bad specs but specs that become misaligned with code.

## Living Specifications as a Solution

Living specs are the most reliable way to guide AI agent development because implementation changes flow back into the specification and prevent spec drift. Living specs produce more reliable agent output than static specs on multi-step tasks with changing requirements or dependencies because bidirectional synchronization keeps the specification aligned with the code as implementation evolves.

Living specs reduce the gap by writing implementation decisions back into the spec, keeping requirements, constraints, and code aligned across repeated development cycles.

## Key Implementation Strategies

Once a specification exists, it must remain synchronized with the codebase by creating an agent skill or hook that analyzes developer prompts and updates spec files before proceeding with implementation.

Specs are living documents in the sense that documentation evolves alongside code rather than decaying in a separate system, residing in the repository and changing with every change to the feature—not as an afterthought, but as a first-class development artifact.

The 2026 ecosystem includes tools like GitHub Spec Kit, AWS Kiro, and others designed specifically to address this synchronization challenge in agentic workflows.

input.content:
Workflow design note ·

Shift the gates left.

Architectural and semantic-model defects — sibling drift, cross-layer round-trip gaps — are cheaper to stop at spec and plan time than to catch in a later proof pass. Three insertions. Two checkpoints. No new agents.

00Baseline

Where the pipeline stands today

A continuous chain, no pause — defects surface only after code is written, reviewed, and committed.

01Proposed

Two gates, folded-in checks

Same agents. Two required pauses, and three new dimensions folded into checkers that already exist.

proof stays — it's the backstop, not the plan

02Evidence

Where three real defects actually got introduced

From this session, not hypotheticals.

Lumen — traced back to origin
DefectIntroduced atWould've been caught by
ClaudeCodeAdapter defaulted to a real, priced model codex.rs already had this exact fix — it never propagated vector — plan Plan task for one SessionAdapter impl, not all four
is_fully_priced hardcoded true on store read-back no column existed; field silently defaulted every round-trip canon — spec Spec never asked "does this field survive the store crate boundary"
tool_counts always empty in shipped output read path shipped; write path never wired canon — spec Same boundary gap — the record type never carried what the read side needed
03Insertions

Three insertions

Language-agnostic — the mechanism differs per stack, the question doesn't.

01

Interface-completeness check

When a task touches one implementer of a shared trait / interface / protocol, the plan must cover every other implementer, or state explicitly why not.

Lives in: vector:challenger, dimension 8 — run as a deterministic pre-scan (grep/AST, TDAD-style dependency graph), not an LLM asked to "remember" siblings. Plain tool call; only its structured output enters the agent's context.
02

Boundary round-trip check

When a criterion introduces a field on a type another spec persists, serializes, or transmits, that far-side spec needs a matching round-trip criterion — or the gap is named on purpose.

Lives in: canon:audit-spec, as a sixth audit dimension alongside its current five.
03

Unrepresentable-by-construction

A value that's sometimes absent, sometimes wrong, or sometimes stale should be a sum type / discriminated union / Result by default — not a bool sitting next to a number. Applies equally to a Rust enum, a TS discriminated union, or a sealed class elsewhere.

Lives in: lambda:implementer's default posture for boundary-crossing fields — reach for this before canon:architect is escalated to, not after.
04Grounding

What the sources actually say

Five findings, each read in full — not a title-only skim — with what it changes here.

Spec-driven development has converged, industry-wide

By 2026 every major AI coding tool — GitHub Spec Kit (93K+ stars, v0.8.7), AWS Kiro, Cursor, Google Antigravity, Tessl — ships some form of spec-driven development, and they've converged on the same shape: specify → plan → tasks → implement. That's graph → canon → vector → lambda, independently arrived at.

Fowler — Understanding SDD: Kiro, spec-kit, Tessl ↗ Validates: the pipeline's shape, not one agent

Living specs beat static ones

Alignment loss during execution caused more failed AI-generated PRs than incorrect task descriptions did — the root cause is specs that stop matching the code, not bad specs. Bidirectional sync closes that gap.

Augment — Living Specs ↗ Changes: canon:correct-spec becomes the default response to contradiction

Self-review is measurably biased

LLMs favor their own output in self-review. The strongest pattern adds a third role — a challenger disproving the checker's own findings, with an arbiter deciding.

Augment — Adversarial Review ↗ Changes: dimensions 01–03 stay in the checker role, never the drafting agent's own pass

Impact analysis should be a graph, not a memory

TDAD builds an explicit dependency map between source files and tests, so before committing, the agent knows exactly which tests a change puts at risk — a queryable graph, not a checklist.

TDAD paper (arXiv 2603.17973) ↗ Changes: insertion 01's implementer scan runs deterministically, before the agent turn

Budget the working set, not the window

Accuracy degrades from ~50K tokens of genuinely relevant context onward, even inside much larger windows. Context editing cut consumption 84% in one 100-turn eval.

Context Is a Budget ↗ GitHub — Token Efficiency ↗ Changes: scans are plain tool calls; gate artifacts show diffs only
05Feedback

Where it already loops back

Feedback paths that exist in this plugin suite today — mostly reactive, worth making automatic.

Existing loop-backs, in detail
LoopCarried byTodayShould trigger on
proof finding → structural fix canon:architect manual routing a defect class recurring ≥2× across siblings
code contradicts spec canon:drafter → vector:planner amend already automatic mid-build keep as default path, not a fallback
spec decays vs. code over time canon:drift-checker on-demand only before extending a spec area untouched N sessions
duplicate / overlapping requirement graph:audit-backlog on-demand only before graph hands a requirement to canon
recurring defect → standing knowledge no formal carrier yet human memory only write back into a lessons doc canon/vector read before drafting
06Human

Where the human sits

Two required pauses — both before a line of implementation code exists.

01
canon drafts + gates a spec
research-report and tradeoffs attached, not just the passing criteria
GATE
Publish spec + tradeoffs as an artifact
short comparison table, not prose — sign-off before vector plans anything
02
vector plans + challenges
interface-completeness check runs here
GATE
Publish plan + task table as an artifact
sign-off before lambda writes anything
03
lambda → axiom → proof run to completion
no further pause — this part was already trustworthy
07Discipline

Token discipline

Tables, not paragraphs

Tradeoffs as a comparison grid. Findings as criterion_id / type / fix rows, matching canon's existing issue format.

One diagram, not a narrative

A plan is a task list a human can scan in ten seconds — not a chat transcript reconstructed as prose.

Flag, don't restate

Checkpoint artifacts show deltas and open questions — never the full spec text the human already saw.

Next

Pick a starting point — vector:challenger, canon:audit-spec, or lambda's default posture — or pilot the two-gate checkpoint manually on the next spec before wiring any of it in.

```
Update three plugin subagent definitions — vector:challenger, canon:audit-spec, and
lambda:implementer — to catch architectural/semantic-model defects (sibling drift across
trait implementers, cross-layer round-trip gaps) at spec/plan time instead of after code
is written. Full rationale and sourced findings: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/8dffec3b-bc4b-4664-a5eb-602c92d40b78

These are Claude Code plugin agent definitions, not part of any project repo — locate them
first (likely markdown files with YAML frontmatter, under wherever `/plugin` installed the
marketplace on this machine — search by agent name, don't assume a path). If you can't find
editable source for one of them, say so plainly instead of reporting success.

Read each target file fully before editing — match its existing structure, tone, and format
exactly. Don't restructure anything unrelated.

Make exactly these three edits:

1. vector:challenger — add an 8th review dimension, "interface-incompleteness": when a task
   modifies one implementer of a shared trait/interface/protocol, the plan must cover every
   other known implementer or explicitly state why not. This check must be backed by a
   deterministic pre-scan (grep/AST enumeration of implementers) run before the agent's own
   reasoning — not an LLM asked to "remember" siblings.

2. canon:audit-spec — add a 6th audit dimension, "boundary round-trip coverage": when a
   criterion introduces or changes a field on a type that another spec persists, serializes,
   or transmits, that far-side spec needs a matching round-trip criterion, or the gap must be
   named on purpose.

3. lambda:implementer — add a default-posture instruction: when a criterion involves a value
   that can be absent, wrong, or stale — especially at a process/crate/serialization boundary
   — prefer a sum type / discriminated union / Result-shaped representation over a raw
   value-plus-boolean pair, in whatever language the task is in. Escalate to canon:architect
```

/rewind

Can we take a look at the current setup for callisto at ~/Projects and see what else we should adjust in terms of moon, cargo or any of our ecosystem setup? Summarize what you find and a proposal.

  This is what michi learned:

  Callisto setup vs. michi's

  Surveyed ~/Projects/callisto (orin-dx/callisto's own repo — same moon+cargo+changesets stack, more mature/battle-tested). Two categories of findings.

  1. A live bug in callisto itself (worth knowing, not michi's to fix)

  callisto's own justfile already has the exact same fix I just applied to michi — lint (single cargo clippy --workspace) + lint-affected (moon-affected-detection → single multi--p invocation), with near-identical comments explaining the lock-contention problem. So callisto's maintainers hit and fixed this before.

  But .github/workflows/callisto-release.yml never got the memo — it calls moon run :format-check/moon run :lint/moon run :test directly, bypassing the fixed justfile recipes entirely. Callisto's own .moon/tasks/rust.yml still defines the raw per-crate -p $project fan-out tasks (dormant, unlike michi's now-deleted ones), so every release-verification run on callisto still pays the lock-serialization tax. callisto-ci.yml (the main CI) correctly uses just lint/just fmt-check/just test — only the release workflow regressed. Michi's own release.yml is unaffected — it calls orin-dx/callisto's callisto-action, which runs callisto status/version/publish directly, never moon run :*.

  2. Patterns callisto has that michi doesn't

  Centralized lints (highest value) — callisto declares lint policy once, in root Cargo.toml:
  [workspace.lints.rust]
  unsafe_code = "forbid"
  unused_must_use = "deny"
  [workspace.lints.clippy]
  all = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }
  map_err_ignore = "deny"
  then each crate opts in with one line: [lints] / workspace = true. Michi instead has this exact block hand-copied at the top of all six lib.rs files:
  #![deny(unsafe_code)]
  #![warn(missing_docs)]
  #![warn(clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::expect_used)]
  #![warn(clippy::disallowed_types)]
  Same policy, 6x duplicated, invisible from Cargo.toml, and drifts silently if one file gets updated and the others don't. Rust 1.74+ feature (michi's MSRV is 1.96) — straightforward to consolidate. One nuance: michi's unsafe_code needs to stay deny (overridable), not callisto's forbid, since CLAUDE.md explicitly allows unsafe at the NAPI boundary via local #[allow].

  cargo-semver-checks — callisto runs cargo semver-checks check-release as just check-api. Michi has no mechanical enforcement of its own documented SemVer contract (docs/spec/05-scope-and-quality.md's Patch/Minor/Major table) — which is exactly the gap that let four breaking changes land without changesets this session. This is the single highest-leverage addition given what we just found.

    set -euo pipefail
    projects=$(moon query projects --affected 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.projects[].id')
    if [ -z "$projects" ]; then

## Callisto vs. Lumen — ecosystem setup

Surveyed `~/Projects/callisto`'s justfile, Cargo.toml, deny.toml, `.moon/tasks/rust.yml`, and CI workflows against Lumen's equivalents.

### Already matches — no action
- **Centralized `[workspace.lints]`** — Lumen's `Cargo.toml:75-91` is near-identical to callisto's (`unsafe_code`, `unused_must_use`, the same clippy allow/deny set through `map_err_ignore`), plus 3 extra cast-lint allows. Already consolidated, not duplicated per-crate. Nothing to do here.
- **Layer-licensing containment** (`deny.toml` bans check via `.moon/tasks/rust.yml`'s `deny` task) — Lumen actually has more here than callisto: a bans-based check enforcing lumen-model/lumen-session never depend on the FSL-licensed crates. Callisto doesn't need this (single license). Lumen-specific strength, not a gap.

### Gap 1 — lint/test still pay the lock-contention tax callisto already fixed for itself
Lumen's `justfile` `lint`/`test` call `moon run :lint` / `moon run :test`, which fan out through `.moon/tasks/rust.yml` to one `cargo clippy -p $project` / `cargo test -p $project` **per crate** (7 separate processes), all locking the same shared `target/` dir. Callisto's own justfile has this exact bug, already fixed, with a comment explaining it:

```
# Moon's per-project `cargo clippy -p $project` tasks all lock the same shared
# target/ dir, so running them one-per-project serializes on Cargo's own build
# lock instead of parallelizing — a single --workspace invocation lets Cargo's
# internal job scheduler parallelize across crates instead.
lint:
    cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

Callisto's `test` similarly prefers `cargo nextest run --workspace` (falling back to moon) over the per-crate fan-out. `cargo-nextest` is already installed locally (`~/.cargo/bin/cargo-nextest`).

**Proposal:** mirror callisto's `lint` + `lint-affected` recipes, and switch `test` to nextest-first with moon fallback.

### Gap 2 — no unused-dependency check, and this bit us already
This session's own audit found 6 unused dependencies across 3 crates (rayon/memmap2 in lumen-analysis, smallvec/tracing in lumen-store, simd-json/memmap2 in lumen-session) — found by manual review. `cargo-machete` (already installed) catches exactly this class of drift automatically. Callisto runs it as `just machete`.

**Proposal:** add `just machete: cargo machete`, wire into `ci:`.

### Explicitly not recommending — cargo-semver-checks
Callisto's whole purpose is changeset/version management, so SemVer enforcement is load-bearing there. Lumen doesn't publish any crate externally yet — pre-release, single consumer. Standing project memory from earlier this session (the ReadContractEnvelope/migration-chain build-then-revert) is specifically about not building premature versioning scaffolding before a real consumer exists. Adding SemVer gating now would be the same mistake in a new shape. Revisit if/when a Lumen crate actually gets published.

### Lower priority
- **`doc-check`** (`RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --workspace`) — cheap, callisto has it, Lumen doesn't. Given how thorough Lumen's doc comments already are, this catches broken intra-doc links for free.
- **`cargo-mutants`** — already installed, and Lumen already gets mutation testing via the `lambda:mutator` agent during implementation. A standalone `just mutants` would just make it repeatable outside that workflow. Already substantially covered.
- **`cargo-llvm-cov` coverage reporting** — callisto has it in CI, Lumen doesn't. Nice-to-have, not a known gap.
- **Dead config**: `rust-toolchain.toml` targets `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, but nothing in any Cargo.toml or doc references wasm anywhere in the repo. Either leftover template config or a real future direction — worth asking rather than silently dropping.

### Proposal, in order
1. Fix the lint/test lock-contention (mirror callisto's validated fix)
2. Add `cargo-machete` (directly closes a gap we already paid for once)
3. Add `doc-check` (cheap, matches callisto)
4. Skip `cargo-semver-checks` for now — revisit at first real publish
5. Ask about the dead `wasm32` toolchain target

Want me to implement 1–3 now?
We will start publishing soon so we should not skip semver checks I think but we definitely don't need wasm here right?

Good calls on both:

- **Semver-checks**: worth noting one mechanical detail — `cargo semver-checks check-release` diffs against the last **published** crates.io version, so it'll have nothing to compare against until each crate's first publish (no-op or error on a never-published crate). Wiring it in now is still the right call — it goes live starting with each crate's second release, and you want the recipe in place before the first one, not scrambling to add it after.
- **wasm**: confirmed — grepped every `Cargo.toml` and both doc files, zero references to `wasm` anywhere in the repo. Safe to drop.

22	# Single workspace invocation. Moon's per-project `cargo clippy -p $project` tasks
23	# (.moon/tasks/rust.yml) all lock the same shared target/ dir, so running them
24	# one-per-project serializes on Cargo's own build lock instead of parallelizing --
25	# a single --workspace invocation lets Cargo's internal job scheduler parallelize
26	# across crates instead. Same fix callisto already applied to its own justfile.
27	lint:
28	    cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
29	
30	# Lint only projects affected by changes since the base branch, still via one
31	# cargo invocation (not moon's per-project fan-out) to avoid the same build-lock
32	# serialization while skipping unaffected crates entirely.
33	lint-affected:
34	    #!/usr/bin/env bash
35	    set -euo pipefail
36	    projects=$(moon query projects --affected 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.projects[].id')
37	    if [ -z "$projects" ]; then
38	        echo "No projects affected — skipping lint."
39	        exit 0
40	    fi
41	    args=()
42	    for p in $projects; do args+=(-p "$p"); done
43	    cargo clippy "${args[@]}" --all-targets -- -D warnings
44	
45	# ── Licensing / Dependency Policy ────────────────────────────────────────────
46	deny:
47	    moon run :deny
48	
49	# Unused-dependency check. Directly closes the gap that let 6 unused deps across
50	# 3 crates (rayon/memmap2, smallvec/tracing, simd-json/memmap2) go unnoticed
51	# until a manual audit found them.
52	machete:
53	    cargo machete
54	
55	# ── API Surface ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
56	# Verifies public API changes against the last-published crates.io version.
57	# NOT wired into `ci:` yet: cargo-semver-checks needs a published baseline to
58	# diff against, and no Lumen crate has been published yet -- running this
59	# before a first publish exists just fails with no baseline. Wire into `ci:`
60	# once the first crate is on crates.io; until then, run manually pre-release.
61	check-api:
62	    cargo semver-checks check-release
63	
64	# Documentation build check (warnings treated as errors) -- catches broken
65	# intra-doc links for free.
66	doc-check:
67	    RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --workspace
68	
69	# ── Pricing Data (CRIT-LUMEN-170) ────────────────────────────────────────────
70	# Refreshes the vendored LiteLLM pricing snapshot lumen-model's PricingTable::seed() loads at
71	# compile time. Never fetched live -- Lumen prices historical sessions and needs point-in-time-
72	# stable rates, so this is a periodic, explicit re-vendor step, not a per-request fetch. Review
73	# the diff (especially any rate change for a currently-seeded model) before committing.
74	update-pricing:
75	    curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/main/model_prices_and_context_window.json \
76	        -o crates/lumen-model/data/litellm_model_prices.json
77	
78	fmt:
79	    moon run :format
80	
81	format: fmt
82	
83	fmt-check:
84	    moon run :format-check
85	
86	# ── Continuous Development & Clean ──────────────────────────────────────────
87	clean:
88	    moon clean 2>/dev/null || true
89	    cargo clean
90	
91	# ── Git Hooks & Pre-push ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
92	pre-commit: fmt-check
93	
94	pre-push: fmt-check lint-affected
95	
96	hooks:
97	    @echo '#!/bin/sh\njust pre-commit' > .git/hooks/pre-commit
98	    @chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
99	    @echo '#!/bin/sh\njust pre-push' > .git/hooks/pre-push
100	    @chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-push
101	    @echo "Git pre-commit and pre-push hooks installed successfully."
102	
103	# ── CI Verification Pipeline ───────────────────────────────────────────────
104	ci: fmt-check lint deny machete doc-check test

Compared Lumen's build tooling against `~/Projects/callisto` and hardened it, 3 commits:

1. **`7c8e615`** — Fixed the same lint/test lock-contention bug callisto already found and fixed (per-crate `moon run :lint`/`:test` fan-out serializing on Cargo's shared build lock → single `--workspace` invocation, `nextest` for tests). Dropped the dead `wasm32-unknown-unknown` toolchain target.
2. **`570d62c`** — `cargo-machete` immediately found 16 unused deps (not 6) across 5 crates. Spot-checked the surprising ones against real source before touching anything, confirmed zero false positives, removed all 16. Full workspace build (including tests/benches) and all 190 tests verified green after.
3. **`1644800`** — `doc-check` found 3 real doc-build errors (two broken intra-doc links to private items, one doc comment parsed as an unclosed HTML tag). Fixed.

`just ci` runs clean end to end. Memory updated with the findings and the `check-api` follow-up so it's not forgotten at first publish.

Any outstanding bugs we've identified? Do we do another round of adversarial analysis looking for bugs? We're finding a lot which is weird given our plugins and our SDD workflow. That shouldnt' be happeneing. Did we not research appropriately? Are our specs not good enough? What's going on

**Current bug status:** No known live bugs remain from the original audit backlog — everything HIGH/MEDIUM found on 2026-08-22 is fixed and committed (6 commits, 190/190 tests, clippy/fmt/deny clean). What's left is a short low-priority cleanup list (minor allocations, a shared JSONL helper, unused deps) — nothing urgent.

But the underlying question — why does this project keep finding bugs despite specs and plugins — deserves a real answer, not reassurance. Three distinct root causes, not one:

**1. A real research gap, but an old one, not a new one.** OpenCodeAdapter was originally built against a "100% fictional JSONL format" (per this project's own memory) — someone wrote an adapter for a wire format they never actually fetched and inspected. That's not a spec-quality failure, it's a research-discipline failure: nothing in canon/vector/lambda forces you to go get a real sample before writing acceptance criteria against it. This class of bug (assumed-vs-real external formats) is basically eliminated now — everything fixed recently was checked against real captured data or a real upstream source (LiteLLM's actual pricing file, real local session logs).

**2. A structural blind spot in the SDD workflow: cross-layer round-trip invariants.** The two bugs I found *today* (`is_fully_priced` silently dropped by the SQL store, `tool_counts` always empty) weren't found by adversarial bug-hunting — they were found by tracing every real call site of a field while implementing an unrelated criterion. Specs here are written and gated per-subsystem (a criterion lives in SPEC-LUMEN-001-MODEL or SPEC-LUMEN-003-STORE, and axiom's exit-gate checks that spec in isolation). Nobody ever wrote a criterion of the shape "field X, once computed, must survive ingest → persist → read → display unchanged" — so no gate ever checked it, because the *question* didn't exist yet, not because the gate failed at its job. `proof`'s hazard-taxonomy scanner is also oriented toward local code shapes (unwraps, injection, resource handling), not "does this field silently vanish three files away in a different crate." That's a real gap in what gets checked, not a broken process.

**3. Normal early-stage entropy.** The domain model (`lumen-model`) and the persistence layer (`lumen-store`) evolved somewhat independently — `SessionFactRecord` didn't even carry tool-call data until today. Fields get added to one layer before the other catches up; nobody notices until someone actually reads the full pipeline end to end.

So: specs aren't bad, and the plugins aren't malfunctioning — but there's a category of bug (cross-subsystem round-trip loss) that this workflow structurally doesn't check for automatically. That's worth closing.

**Recommendation:** not a generic re-run of `proof` — it already ran, and this bug class would slip past it again for the same structural reason. What's actually worth doing is a targeted pass asking, for every field on `TokenEconomics`/`CanonicalTranscript` that has a store column: *does it survive ingest → persist → read → display, with a test proving it, not just an inspection*. Want me to run that now?
I'm not just worried about those pieces, I'm worries about the whole codebase. Architecture, performance stance and analysis, security, DX, semantic model, etc

A whole-codebase sweep across architecture, performance, security, DX, and semantic model is a legitimately large undertaking for a multi-crate Rust workspace this size (~7 crates, several thousand lines). Worth being clear about what's already been covered versus what's genuinely new ground:

**Already covered (2026-08-22, one comprehensive multi-agent audit):** architecture, security, performance, DX, and bugs — 17 findings raised, 16 confirmed and adversarially verified. All of those either got fixed already or turned into spec criteria that are now also fixed (pricing vendoring, redaction rewrite, the adapter contract, the `Cost` type, the round-trip bugs, the tool-call wiring). What's genuinely untouched from that audit is just the low-priority bucket (minor allocations, unused deps, a shared JSONL helper) and the layer-licensing dev-dependency question.

**Not really covered yet:** the *semantic model* specifically — whether the domain types (`CanonicalTranscript`, `TokenEconomics`, `ToolIntent`, the adapter abstraction itself) are the right shapes for what this project is actually trying to represent, versus just internally consistent. That's a different, harder kind of review than "find bugs in the code as written."

Given the scope you're describing, I have two real options, and the cost difference matters enough that I don't want to just pick one:

1. **A proper multi-agent Workflow** — one phase per dimension (architecture, perf, security, DX, semantic model), each with its own finder(s), then an adversarial verification pass on every finding before anything gets reported, the same shape as the 2026-08-22 audit. This is thorough and catches things a single pass misses, but it's a real token spend across potentially dozens of subagent calls — this needs your explicit go-ahead to run (say "use a workflow" and I'll kick it off).
2. **A lighter pass I run myself** via a few parallel forks, one per dimension, without the adversarial verification layer — faster and cheaper, but more likely to surface plausible-but-wrong findings since nothing double-checks them.

Given you're asking about the whole codebase and seem to want real confidence, not a quick look, I'd lean toward option 1. Want me to run it as a workflow — and if so, any dimension you want weighted heaviest (semantic model sounds like the one that's actually novel here)?

**Findings:**

1. **The layer-licensing ban is not actually enforced for the known dev-dependency gap — this is a real, live gap, not just theoretical.** `deny.toml`'s `[bans].deny` list only bans `lumen-analysis` and `lumen-pattern` (`deny.toml:29-32`). But the file's own `[licenses]` comment (`deny.toml:38-40`) states `lumen-store` is *also* FSL-1.1-MIT and Layer 2. `lumen-session/Cargo.toml:20` lists `lumen-fixtures` as a dev-dependency, and `lumen-fixtures/Cargo.toml:11` depends on `lumen-store`. So `lumen-session` (Layer 1.5, promised MIT/Apache-2.0) transitively pulls FSL-licensed `lumen-store` code into its dev-dependency graph — exactly the scenario the top-of-file comment says must never happen — and `cargo-deny check bans` would pass cleanly because `lumen-store`/`lumen-fixtures` were never added to the `deny` array. The enforcement mechanism has a hole matching its own documented threat model. **High confidence.** Fix is mechanical: add `lumen-store` and `lumen-fixtures` entries to `[bans].deny` (with an appropriate `wrappers` list, or accept the dev-only exposure explicitly and document why it's fine — but right now nothing decided either way, it's just unenforced).

2. **`SessionAdapter` is not a uniform abstraction across all 4 providers — `OpenCodeAdapter` doesn't implement it.** `lumen-session/src/adapters/opencode.rs:8-14`'s doc comment explains why: OpenCode's real backing store is SQLite, structurally incompatible with `parse_stream(Box<dyn BufRead>)`. `OpenCodeAdapter` instead exposes its own `parse_database(&Path) -> Result<Vec<CanonicalTranscript>, IngestionError>`, and `lumen-cli/src/main.rs:124` special-cases it with an explicit `match` arm rather than dispatching through the trait. This is self-documented and not silently broken (no dispatcher assumes uniformity), but it means the trait boundary was designed around a JSONL-stream assumption that one of four real-world adapters can't satisfy — any future adapter with a similarly non-stream-shaped source (a REST API, another SQLite/DB-backed tool) will face the same fork. Worth deciding now whether `SessionAdapter` should be generalized (e.g., an enum-returning entry point that both stream- and DB-backed adapters implement) rather than accumulating special cases in the CLI. **Medium-high confidence this is a real design smell; not currently causing a bug.**

3. **`lumen-model` → `lumen-store` direction is clean; no violation found.** Checked `lumen-model/Cargo.toml` — zero storage/SQL dependencies, `lumen-model` has no knowledge of persistence concerns. Correct direction, no coupling. Not a finding, stated for completeness since it was explicitly in scope.
